verdict: OK to lend in Rajkot auto components — pursue Tier-2 precision and EV/drone-motor makers with tight covenants; avoid single-OEM, ICE-engine-dependent units.
title: Rajkot Auto & Auto Components: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Rajkot's auto-component cluster is a machining-and-forging town: small units turning castings and bar stock into shafts, gears, brackets and sub-assemblies for OEMs.** Cash comes from converting metal into parts on a job-work or supply basis, so the cycle is short on the shop floor but long on the receivable — OEM payment terms stretch the working-capital cycle well past the production cycle. **Value sits in the tooling and the OEM approval, not the machine**, which is why a unit with a locked-in part number has pricing power and one chasing open tenders does not.

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is strong and national: IIP for auto components (NIC 29) is +25.2% YoY and +19.2% Apr-to-date [D].** Gujarat is pulling ahead of the country on consumption — GST collections +11.9% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D]. **But bank credit is running at +27.0% YoY against output of +19.2%, a gap of +7.8 pp [D]** — money is entering the chain faster than parts are leaving it, so when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower's own sales growth matches the credit it is asking for; if the ask outruns output, ask what the extra limit is actually funding. Peer results confirm volume strength but flag margin squeeze from aluminium [3] and commodity risk [5], so **price the commodity pass-through clause, not just the volume story.**

## Where the growth is
**Pursue the precision and new-mobility suppliers: EV-component and lightweighting order wins are real at the peer level [3], and Rajkot has a genuine deep-tech edge — a local startup's indigenous drone motors were the only Gujarat manufacturing pick for Bharat Innovates 2026 in France [1].** That is a local-news signal, not audited financials, so treat it as a door-opener, not a credit case. **Avoid units concentrated on engine and engine-related parts** — rating commentary flags higher obsolescence risk as EVs spread [10]. **Rajkot-specific financial data is thin in these sources; lean on first principles and the peer read.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the receivable, not the machine: gross current assets have averaged 160-170 days in this sector [9], so size the drawing power to that cycle and take the OEM purchase order as the base.** Take monthly stock-and-debtor statements, monthly GST returns, and a quarterly ageing of receivables by OEM. **Set a Debt/EBITDA ceiling of 2.5-2.75 times as the outer limit [9]** and covenant that any debt-funded capex above plan needs prior consent. For the drone/EV names, ask for the customer contract and collect from customer the current order book and receivable days before sanctioning.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch the credit-to-output gap at the borrower level: if receivables stretch beyond the sector's 160-170 day norm [9], cut limits.** If a unit's sales flatten while its bank limit utilisation stays full, the extra money is funding someone else's delay — ask for the OEM payment confirmation. If aluminium or commodity costs rise without a pass-through clause [3][5], margin will absorb it; reprice or reduce exposure. If a borrower's part numbers are engine-linked, start the exit conversation early [10].
watch: GST turnover falls below reported sales -> ask for OEM invoices and freeze enhancement
Receivables cross 170 days [9] -> cut drawing power and seek OEM payment confirmation
Crosses 2.5-2.75x [9] -> stop new limits, restructure to receivable-backed only
Aluminium cost rises with no pass-through [3][5] -> reprice or reduce exposure
Engine-linked parts dominate the order book [10] -> begin exit or demand diversification plan
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
